question: The rule of law is a universal principle of governance that is fundamental to international peace, security and political stability. As part of the development of rule of law policy at EU level, in 2014, the Commission issued a communication on the new EU framework to strengthen the rule of law, recognising it as a constitutional principle and setting out a nonexhaustive list of its key elements.

In 2019, the rule of law was further defined, and, in December 2020, the EU co-legislators (the European Parliament and the Council) established a legally binding definition of the rule of law under the Conditionality Regulation (Article 2). In its official report 2025:99, the Swedish Government proposed a special law allowing for the blanket revocation of permanent residence permits.

The proposal would mean that previously favourable administrative decisions could be retroactively amended to the detriment of the individual. According to the principle of legality, however, public powers must be exercised in a predictable and clearly regulated manner.

Several consultative bodies have rejected the proposal, arguing that it runs counter to the fundamental principles of the rule of law, international law and the principle of the best interests of the child. 1.

Does the Commission consider the retroactive blanket revocation of permanent residence permits that have already been granted to be compatible with legal certainty and the fundamental principles of the rule of law?
Does the Commission consider the proposal to be compatible with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the Treaty on European Union?
Does the Commission intend to take action and, if so, what would such action entail?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.5.2026) The Commission generally does not comment on draft legislation. Accordingly, it is not in a position to provide an answer to the questions submitted by the Honourable Members.
